title: Mountains closing in
hookLine: aging and death roll in on King Pasenadi like mountains from four sides (SN 3.25)

cards: It's the middle of the day. King Pasenadi of Kosala arrives to see the Buddha. Where have you come from, great king?

And the king, with surprising honesty, says: from the business of being king. The sort of affairs kings get absorbed in: drunk on power, greedy for pleasure, settled in their country, ruling more land.
The Buddha doesn't scold him. He asks him to imagine something. A messenger arrives from the east, someone you trust completely.

teach.h: A MOUNTAIN FROM THE EAST, HIGH AS CLOUDS
teach.b: Here's the scene from SN 3.25. The messenger says: your majesty, I've come from the east. A great mountain, high as the clouds, is moving this way, crushing every living thing in its path.
Do what you think best. A second messenger comes from the west with the same news. A third from the north.
Four mountains, rolling in from four sides. If that happened, the Buddha asks, what should you do? Pasenadi doesn't hesitate.
What else, except to live by the Dhamma, to act rightly, to do good? The Buddha says: then I tell you, great king, aging and death are rolling in on you. Pasenadi takes stock out loud.

A king has elephant troops, cavalry, chariots, foot soldiers; none can win a battle against aging and death. He has counselors skilled at splitting an enemy with clever schemes; they can't turn them back.

teach.h: NO ARMY, SCHEME OR TREASURE STOPS THEM
teach.b: He has treasure in his vaults; he can't buy them off. So what else is there but to live well and do good?

The Buddha closes with a verse: like huge rock mountains reaching the sky, closing in from all sides, so aging and death come over every living being, warriors, brahmins, workers, everyone. Nobody is spared.

teach.h: THE KING ANSWERS HIS OWN QUESTION
teach.b: The king has just told the Buddha what he spends his days on. The parable doesn't add one fact he didn't know.
It puts the mountains where he can see them, and lets him answer the question himself.

how: Some Buddhists regularly reflect on aging and death, often using the five daily recollections (I am of the nature to age, to sicken, to die, to be parted from what is dear, and heir to my actions), and stories like Pasenadi's mountains are told to frame that reflection.

o: a king's army marching in from four sides
a mountain, the image for aging and death
a messenger bringing news from the east

p: live by the Dhamma, do good

s: the Buddha scolds Pasenadi for being drunk on power
Pasenadi says it himself; the Buddha answers with a parable, not a scolding.
Pasenadi answers the Buddha's question himself
what else could be done, he says, but live rightly and do good.
the king says his clever counselors can turn back aging
he lists armies, counselors and treasure, and says none of them can.

games.q: you're King Pasenadi. four trusted messengers say mountains are rolling in from four sides, crushing everything. what do you do?
o: send the army to stop them.
hide the treasure in the vaults.
live by the Dhamma and do good while you can.
games.why: that's exactly the king's answer, and then the Buddha tells him the mountains are aging and death, already rolling in.

practice: Let the breath slow, and without drama picture time moving in from every side, the way it does for everyone, not to scare yourself, just to see clearly. Then ask the king's question quietly: given that, what matters most?
Don't rush the answer; let something rise, a person, a way of being, a thing left undone, and breathe beside it.

wordCard.voice: Pabbata, mountain. In SN 3.25, aging and death roll in on King Pasenadi like mountains from four sides; no army or treasure can stop them, and what remains is living well. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali pabbata: mountain. SN 3.25 is the Pabbatupama Sutta, the mountain simile.

carryVoice: Your line: what matters most. The king answered his own question: live well, do good. See you tomorrow.
